strings.text: They would run through a wall, and occasionally do.
Nobody has ever described a practice here as pleasant.
Teams hold up better in the late innings.
He would rather build one than buy one.
He gets the kid who was going somewhere else.
Hours on a recruit count for more.
He sends the runner. He has always sent the runner.
His teams are never comfortable and never finished.
Men who sign for him tend to graduate for him.
He knows what the programme did in 1974 and why it mattered.
Prestige builds faster where history is prized.
He will take the pitcher every time, and has.
He has a number for everything and does not move off it.
Arms are worked closer to their limit without going past it.
He has never asked a man to shorten up in his life.
More power out of the same bats.
He has managed every game he was allowed to manage.
Small edge in games taken personally.
He is out of that dugout before the second walk.
Bunt, run, take the extra base, go home.
Steals and bunts land more often.
Freshmen get innings here, and everybody knows it.
Almost nobody leaves early, and it is not an accident.
He knows what every programme in the country is doing.
His teams have won too many games they had no business in.
The bus does not bother him and it does not bother them.
Every roster he has been given finished above where it started.
Prestige rises faster on a good year.
Men who were leaving have a coffee with him and stay.
Better odds of talking a man out of the draft.
Two men have been sacked here with winning records.
They will tell you about 1974 before they tell you where your office is.
Sign a bat and the pitching coach will want a word.
Nobody here has ever been in a hurry, including the board.
Swing hard. The wind off the water does the rest.
Nobody arrives finished. Everybody leaves better or leaves early.
They sign men nobody scouted and are quietly smug about it.
The fence is close and the philosophy is closer.
The water takes its time. So does the board.
Nobody here is above carrying something.
Four years, a degree, and a hard nine innings.
They have never bought a player and do not intend to start.
A regional is a disappointment they are too polite to name.
Blazers in the stands and a century of minutes in a cabinet.
They want the best kid in Florida and they usually get him.
They will forgive a loss. They will not forgive a lazy one.
Thin air, long practices, and a genuine belief that it matters.
They would rather have three arms than one bat.
Men who leave early are spoken about carefully and not warmly.
They find them where nobody else is looking.
Steal a base, steal a game, steal somebody else’s recruit.
A quiet place that plays aggressive baseball.
Legs, wind, and a groundskeeper who cuts the grass short.
Half the coaches in the country took their first job here.
A trophy case, and a list of everyone who failed to add to it.
Every banner has a man who hung it, and they know all their names.
They will ask about your defensive alignment before your record.
They would rather try something and be wrong than be late.
Nothing here has ever come up easy and they prefer it that way.
Good grades, good gloves, and no fuss about either.
The ball carries here, and so does the philosophy.
Four years, or do not bother knocking.
Rain, reps, and a bullpen that throws all winter.
They have not signed a rated recruit in eleven years. On purpose.
Patient, quiet, and unusually good at stealing a game.
If it is on the ground, somebody here is already running.
Founded by men who dug it out, and they never stop saying so.
Four coaches in fifty years. They liked three of them.
The wind blows out, and forty years of baseball is built on it.
Scouting is the whole religion here.
They want it played properly and will tell you when it was not.
Six months indoors makes pitchers. They have the record to prove it.
They gamble. It has cost them, and they keep doing it.
One crop a year, and everybody is expected to be there for it.
Bunt, run, take the extra base, go home.
They keep the ones who last the winter.
Never ranked, and never a losing decade.
Men pass through on the way somewhere. Both directions.
Nine men, one plan, and no room for a passenger.
First to third on anything. They will not apologise for an out.
Every man on the roster is from within four hours of here.
Thin air, hard throwers, and a staff that likes both.
Nobody expects anything here, which is exactly how they like it.
Long bus rides, and no complaining about them.
They play more baseball in a year than anybody in the country.
Nobody wants to come here in May, and they know it.
Deep fences, deep counts, deep patience.
No winning season since 1998, and the stands are still full.
Speed is cheaper than power, and they made a philosophy of it.
Nothing happens fast here. That is the entire pitch.
Big rosters, long seasons, and no interest in shortcuts.
They will lose two-one and call it a good night out.
Take the raw thing, heat it, and see what it becomes.
They keep more numbers than anybody, and read all of them.
Nothing about being here is easy, starting with February.
They recruit places nobody else will drive to.
One oar out of time and the whole thing turns.
Cold, loud, and unreasonably hard to beat at home.
Nobody plays one position here for four years.
Small ball, small budget, small complaints.
They judge a coach on his fourth year, not his first.
Nobody is recruited here. Everybody is made here.
Altitude, attitude, and a fence nobody clears cheaply.
They mine. They do not shop.
The pitching lab keeps better hours than the library.
Nobody outruns them and nobody outlasts them.
Quiet, remote, and deeply suspicious of anybody in a hurry.
A small school that plays like it has just been insulted.
Men graduate here. All four years, every time.
They have lost more of them than anybody, and learned from it.
A century of hard work, and no apologies for the record.
They will give a coach six years. They will also notice all six.
The hardest place in the country to win, and they know it.
Nobody has ever expected anything, so anything is a triumph.
Old school, old money, and a very long memory.
They have waited forty years and are prepared to wait longer.
Defence first, and they will say it twice.
Hard hours, no shortcuts, and a suspicion of anybody polished.
Somebody has done this job for a century without any fuss.
They take the men who were passed over, and work them.
They rebuild swings from nothing. Some of them survive it.
The bus rides are the recruiting pitch. They are honest about it.
Nothing dramatic has happened here, and nothing is expected to.
Hard, slow and hot. Ask anybody who played here.
They build a roster the way they built the town. Slowly.
Every coach here is on the way up or on the way out. Both are welcome.
Ninth, down one. Man on first. Best hitter up, fastest man on the bench.
Bunt him over. A run is a run.
He swings. He is my best hitter for a reason.
Pinch run first. Worry about the bat after.
I would have used the fast man in the eighth.
Two recruits, one week. One is ready now. One is two years away.
The one who is ready. I am judged on Junes, not on projects.
The project. I would rather build one than buy one.
Whichever one wants to be here in four years.
I sign both and let them work it out on the field.
A senior who started three years is now fourth choice. He knows.
He starts. You do not take that off a man in his last year.
He sits, and I tell him myself before he hears it.
He sits. The lineup is not a reward for service.
He plays the position he can still play, not the one he had.
Eighty-nine pitches, one-run lead, seventh. Velocity down two.
He is out. The number is the number.
He finishes the inning. He has earned that much.
I go and ask him, and I believe what his face says.
He is out, and he was out at eighty.
Money for one thing: the cage, an indoor mound, or scouting.
The cages. Every man on the roster uses them every day.
The mound. Arms are the only thing I cannot manufacture.
Scouting. I would rather see them early than fix them late.
None of it. I put it toward the men who are already here.
Four straight losses. The dugout is quiet. Somebody has to speak.
That it is on me, and that I will fix it.
Nothing. They are grown men and they know.
That we are going to run until somebody remembers how.
One thing each, quietly, to four different men.
A bigger school has called your best bat. He has not said no.
I tell him what he is worth here and let him decide.
I tell him to go, and I mean it.
I have already called the man who would replace him.
I ask him what the other school promised, and I beat it.
31-24 got your predecessor sacked. 22-33 got the man before a fourth year.
What does that tell you about this job?
That the record is not the thing they are counting.
That somebody upstairs liked one of them.
Nothing I can use. I will be judged on my own.
That I should ask what the fourth year was for.
Down three in the eighth. Fastest man on first, nobody out.
No. You do not make the first out at second down three.
He is going. He is going most of the time.
Only if the catcher has shown me something.
He decides. That is what I recruited him for.
A walk-on has outplayed a signed freshman all fall. Not close.
Who opens the season at that position?
The walk-on. The fall is what the fall is for.
The freshman. He was signed for a reason and it is February.
The walk-on, and I tell the freshman exactly why.
Whoever is still ahead in April. Fall ball is not a season.
Two men broke curfew before a regional. One is your closer.
Both sit. It is not a rule if it bends for the closer.
Both play, and both run until they are sick on Monday.
They tell the room themselves. Then I decide.
Nothing today. We are playing a regional today.
Your best arm is one exam from ineligible. He told nobody.
With me. I should have known six weeks ago.
With him. He is twenty and it is one exam.
With whoever recruited a man who hides things.
Nowhere yet. Somebody sits with him tonight and it gets fixed.
The rivalry is Friday, a seed on the line Sunday. One ace.
Friday. Ask anybody in this town which game matters.
Sunday. The seed is worth three of Friday.
Friday, three innings, and Sunday on short rest.
Neither. Somebody else is ready and this is how we find out.
Your own crowd is booing a freshman shortstop. It is April.
What do you do about it?
He stays out there. He comes off when I say, not when they do.
I move him to second where the throw is shorter.
I say something about it publicly. Once.
Nothing. He will hear worse in a regional.
The man who paid for the outfield wall has a nephew. Not a player.
He can have a jacket and a seat on the bus. Not a spot.
No, and I tell the donor myself rather than let it travel.
He walks on like anybody else and the fall decides it.
He is on the roster. The wall is still up next year.
He closes the folder. The one question he actually wrote down.
Why do you want this job?
Because I can win here, and I do not think you know that yet.
Because I would like to be here in fifteen years.
Because somebody has to fix this and I would enjoy it.
Because it is the best job that would have me. You knew that.
You think the steal is on. A pitchout makes it three and one.
Yes. I would rather be wrong at three and one than beaten.
No. Three and one is how you lose the inning without a steal.
No, but the catcher knows to expect it and that is enough.
Yes, and if I am wrong I will call it again next inning.
Three errors in two games. He is still your best defender.
More ground balls. Two hundred a day until his hands remember.
A day off. His hands are fine and his head is not.
He plays through it. Nobody ever fixed this from a bench.
I look at where he is standing before I look at his hands.
Your cleanup hitter is three for forty. Still your best hitter.
Does he move in the order?
No. He is the best hitter and the order is not a mood ring.
He drops to sixth for a week and nobody makes a speech.
He leads off. Get him four at-bats and stop thinking about it.
He sits two games and we look at video neither of us enjoys.
Doubleheader tomorrow, one rested arm. Game two is the better team.
Game one. Win the one you can and see what happens.
Game two. I am not conceding a game before it is played.
Neither. Three innings in each and the pen covers the rest.
Game one, and whoever is best in game two earns game one next week.
The chart says shift. Your shortstop has hated it for eleven years.
The chart. He can hate it from the correct side of the bag.
He does. A man who is uncomfortable does not make that play.
The chart, after he has seen it and told me it is wrong.
Nobody. We shift for the two hitters it actually matters against.
One scholarship. A catcher for four years, or a shortstop for two.
The catcher. Four years of a starter is four years.
The shortstop. Two years of that changes the programme.
The catcher, and I find the shortstop money somewhere else.
Whichever one I can still make better in eighteen months.
He wants to play through it. The trainer says it costs three weeks.
No. Three weeks in May is worth more than tonight.
Yes. He asked, he is an adult, and he knows the trade.
Not tonight. We will talk again on Friday and mean it.
Yes, and I hold him to five innings whatever he says after.
Four straight losses. A reporter asks, on the record, about your job.
That anybody in this job who is not worried is not paying attention.
That I am worried about Friday, which is the honest answer.
That he should ask the athletic director, and I mean it kindly.
That the men in that room have not quit, so neither have I.
Your best assistant has a head job offer. He asks what you think.
Take it. Nobody gets a second one of these.
Stay a year. You will get a better one and I will help.
That I would rather he stayed, which is not advice.
Whatever he wants to hear. He has already decided.
Your best player in October is a freshman. The room is watching.
Third, from the first game. The room can watch him earn it.
Ninth, and he moves up when he stops being a freshman.
Seventh. High enough to matter, low enough to breathe.
Wherever the seniors say, once, and then wherever I say.
Up eleven in the seventh. Their freshman is having an awful day.
Nothing different. We play until it is over.
Bench empties. Everybody who travelled gets an at-bat.
Nobody runs and nobody swings three-nothing. They will remember.
My pitcher gets his innings. He needs them more than I need mercy.
Rain in twenty minutes. You are ahead in the fifth, so it counts.
How do you play the next ten minutes?
Quickly. Everybody hacks and nobody steps out.
Exactly as we would at nought-nought in the first.
Slowly, and I will hear about it, and it will be worth it.
I get my arm out before the delay rather than after.
Two men enter the portal. One never played. One started forty games.
The one who never played. That one is mine.
The starter. Forty games buys a conversation.
Neither. Men leave. I have two names to call this afternoon.
Both, and I will say so to the room without naming them.
The man you replaced is at every home game, in the same seat.
What do you do with that?
I ask him to lunch in the first week.
Nothing. He bought a ticket like everybody else.
I put him to work. He knows every family within a hundred miles.
I leave his banner where it is and never mention it again.
Two men can lead off. One gets on base. One is the fastest here.
The one who gets on. You cannot steal first.
The fast one. He changes what their pitcher is thinking about.
The one who gets on, and the fast one hits behind him.
Whichever one takes the most pitches. I want their starter tired.
Eleven hours on a bus, in at four, noon game you should win.
Nothing. They sleep and I let them.
Video. Eleven hours is a gift and we are wasting it.
I sit with three men I have not sat with this year.
Nothing, and nobody complains about the bus. Ever. To anyone.
Your catcher cannot hit. Two of your arms are worse without him.
Every day. What he does is not in the box score.
Not against their best arm. I need nine hitters that night.
Every day, and we fix the bat in the mornings all winter.
Every day, and I stop pretending it is a problem.
A freshman is your third arm and your second bat. He wants both.
Both, carefully, with a number on it that I do not move off.
Both, and we find out. That is what a freshman year is.
He hits. Bats last longer than elbows.
He pitches. I can find a bat and I cannot find that arm.
They want a captain. The obvious man is your worst player.
The one they picked. That is what the vote was for.
Nobody. Twenty-three men and none of them need a letter.
Both, and the quiet one learns something he needs.
The best player. It is a baseball team.
He needs surgery. He would rather rest it and pitch a regional.
Surgery, this week. He has fifteen years of throwing left.
Surgery, and I tell him it was my call so he can be angry at me.
He rests. It is his elbow and his May.
Two doctors first. I am not deciding this off one opinion.
A recruit is on campus with his mother. She asks about graduation.
What does the day look like?
She meets four seniors without me in the room.
The facility, the plan for him, and a number on it.
Whatever the other three are not doing.
Practice, unedited, and then I answer everything she asks.
A father has emailed four times about innings. The son says nothing.
The son, once, and never about the emails.
The father, once, and it will be a short conversation.
Both, together, so nobody can repeat it differently later.
Nobody. I answer with innings or I do not answer.
You are 14-2 and not a 14-2 team. They are saying Omaha out loud.
What do you say about that?
That we are 14-2 and that both those numbers are small.
That we are going, and I would rather be wrong loudly.
Nothing to them. Plenty to the four men who think it is done.
Money for the infield, or money for an assistant. Not both.
The field. Bad hops cost games and confidence, in that order.
The assistant. A man can fix more than a groundskeeper can.
The field. It is the first thing a seventeen-year-old sees.
Neither. Both of those are next year and I need arms now.
New uniforms, and not what the programme has worn since 1961.
The old ones. There is a reason people recognise them.
The new ones. Seventeen-year-olds are not alumni yet.
The old ones at home, the new ones on the road.
Whatever they vote for. It is on their backs.
A juco bat, ready now. A scout you trust says the swing will not hold.
Yes. Two years of ready is worth more than four of maybe.
Yes, and I will fix the swing myself.
No. I trust the scout and I trust four years more.
No. I would rather be wrong about somebody who will be here.
You have just given up nine in an inning. Two left.
A freshman who needs to stand out there once.
Whoever throws strikes. I want this over.
A position player. Nobody warm is worth burning tonight.
My best available. They are not going to enjoy the ninth.
Your class is ranked fortieth. You think it is your best here.
Not to me. It matters to the seventeen-year-olds, so it matters.
No. Rankings measure who else wanted them.
It matters to the board, and the board matters to me.
Ask me in four years and I will give you a real answer.
Six straight wins and the room has gone quiet. You know that quiet.
Yes. Something changes today while we are still winning.
No. You do not go looking for a problem at six in a row.
I ask two seniors what I am missing.
A day off. Nobody has had one since February.
The call was wrong and every man in the park knows it.
I go, and I make sure it is worth going for.
Nothing. I am not spending a suspension on the fourth inning.
A word between innings that nobody in the stands can hear.
I go if a man of mine is about to, and I go first.
A junior is drafted for real money. He asks what you think.
Go. That money does not come round again.
Stay a year and the money doubles. I have seen it twice.
What I would tell my own son, and then I sit down.
That I want him here and that he should ignore me.
Your seed depends on a game three states away, finishing later.
Does the dugout know the score?
No. Phones away. We are playing a game.
Yes. They can count and pretending otherwise is silly.
I know. That is enough for it to change what I call.
Nobody knows, including me, and I mean that.
An assistant of nineteen years was passed over for your job.
What do you do with him?
He keeps everything he had, and I ask him things in front of people.
He runs the pitchers. Nineteen years of those arms is worth having.
He recruits. He knows every coach in three states.
I bring my own man and I tell him that on day one.
Last fall scrimmage. A senior and a freshman, still tied.
The senior opens. Ties go to the man who has been here.
The freshman opens. Ties go to the man with the upside.
Neither. They platoon until one of them stops being tied.
Whoever handles being told he is not starting.
Three years into five, 62-73 here. The board has said nothing.
Nothing. Three years is not long enough to know.
Everything on offence. We are losing the way we have always lost.
The recruiting. I have been signing the wrong men.
I go and ask the board directly what they are counting.
First practice. Twenty-three men, none of them yours, watching.
What is the first thing you do?
Ground balls. We find out where everybody actually is.
I learn twenty-three names and use every one before we start.
I tell them exactly what will get a man on this field.
We run. It is not subtle and it does not need to be.
Four days running for the pen. One-run game, eighth, all lying.
Nobody. The starter finishes what he started.
The one who is lying least convincingly.
The best one. Tomorrow is not my problem tonight.
The one who has thrown fewest pitches, and I look it up.
Four hundred people in a four thousand seat park. You are winning.
Mine. Win enough and they come.
Mine, but not on a Tuesday. Ask me again in May.
Nobody’s. Four hundred people came to watch baseball.
The programme’s, and I will go and speak to every school in the county.
Four years, eleven games, not one missed practice or complaint.
A start on senior day, and I do not make a speech about it.
A job on my staff if he wants one.
Exactly what he has earned, which is what he already had.
Told, in front of the room, what four years of that is worth.
A grad student sends spray charts nobody asked for. Two were right.
What do you do with him?
He gets a desk and a job title.
He keeps sending them and I keep reading them. That is enough.
I ask him what he thinks about the two he got wrong.
Nothing. I have three coaches and a bus to pay for.
Youngest man ever in this chair. Three players are nearly your age.
I raise it first, in the first meeting, and then never again.
No. It comes up the first time I make an unpopular decision.
Constantly, and I will use it. They tell me things.
It comes up with parents, not players. That is the real problem.
The last two men hired in this conference are half your age.
What have you got that they have not?
I have been wrong more times and remember all of them.
Every high school coach in this state takes my call.
Nothing they will not have in ten years. So I had better win now.
I know what a room sounds like before it goes wrong.
Ninety-six at first pitch, ninety-one at the last. Most of your season.
It does not. They live here.
Shorter practices, earlier, and nobody is a hero in July.
My arms throw fewer pitches than anybody in the league.
It is the best thing we have. Visitors wilt in the seventh.
Indoors until March. Your first eleven games are somewhere else.
How do you build a season out of that?
Arms. Six months indoors is the best pitching lab in the country.
Defence. You can take a thousand ground balls on a gym floor.
Recruiting. I sell eleven games in the sun to seventeen-year-olds.
Toughness, and I am aware of how that sounds.
First base open, two out. Their best hitter, man on second.
Yes. I would rather face anybody else on earth.
No. My man gets him out or he learns something.
No. Putting the winning run on is how you lose in the ninth.
Yes, and I would do it in the first inning too.
Man on first, one out. Your hitter has struck out twice already.
Hit and run. Get him moving and take the double play away.
Nothing. Two strikeouts is a reason to let him hit.
Nothing. Two strikeouts is a reason not to ask him to do more.
Straight steal. I trust the legs more than the bat tonight.
Thirty innings now as your fifth arm, or your best arm as a senior.
None. Four years of him is worth more than thirty innings.
Thirty. He needs to stand out there and I need the innings.
He decides, once I have told him the truth about both.
None, and I say the word senior to him every week until it is.
Your best athlete cannot stay at short. He sees no problem.
How does he end up in centre field?
I show him the numbers and let him argue with them.
He plays there in the fall and finds out he likes it.
I tell him. It is my lineup and he is an outfielder.
A scout tells him. He will believe a scout.
You are 4-11. Nothing is broken. You have looked twice.
What do you do this week?
Change the lineup entirely. Something has to move.
Nothing. Fifteen games is fifteen games.
Talk to eleven men individually and listen more than I talk.
Go back to the fundamentals we clearly did not finish in the fall.
Your best player is your worst teammate. Not cruel, just absent.
He sits a game. Once. Everybody understands the rest of the year.
Nothing. He is twenty and he hits. Both of those pass.
I give him something to be responsible for and see what happens.
I ask the seniors to handle it before I have to.
Yours is the deciding vote, and everybody will know how you used it.
The way I think is right, and I will say why out loud.
The way that helps my programme. That is what I am paid for.
With the two coaches I will need something from in June.
I abstain, and I am aware that is also a decision.
The arm nobody can get has asked you for a plan on paper.
Innings. Exactly how many, from week one, in writing.
What he throws in three years that he cannot throw now.
The draft. What he is worth now and what he is worth after.
Nothing. I do not put promises on paper for anybody.
Their pitcher has hit two of yours. The second looked deliberate.
I get in front of them. Nobody on my team gets suspended for this.
Nothing today. It gets remembered and it gets returned in May.
It gets returned in the bottom of this inning.
I am the first one out there and the loudest.
A freshman has not spoken in six weeks. A thousand miles from home.
I put him with a senior from his part of the country.
I play him. Nothing fixes homesick like being needed.
I sit with him. Not about baseball, and not once.
I leave him alone. Some men need six weeks and not a speech.
A rival has offered your best assistant nearly what you make.
I tell the board to find it, and I mean it as an ultimatum.
I give him everything I can that is not money.
I help him go, and I have already got two names.
I offer him my job in five years, and I am not joking.
Eleventh, everybody has pitched, and a first baseman is warming.
How do you play the twelfth?
We are trying to win it this inning, by any means available.
Exactly as we played the first. Nothing changes because it is late.
I protect the first baseman. He has a season after tonight.
Every man left on the bench is in the game by the thirteenth.
Your best hitter wants summer ball for a coach you do not know.
Go. Four hundred at-bats is four hundred at-bats.
Not there. I will find him somewhere I can watch.
Go, and I will call that coach on Sunday and every Sunday.
Stay. Three months here is worth more than four hundred at-bats.
Somebody hits ninth: a light-hitting shortstop, or a freshman.
The freshman. Ninth is the best place to learn to hit here.
The shortstop. Ninth is where the worst hitter goes.
The shortstop, and he is a second leadoff man in front of the top.
Neither. Ninth is for whoever had the worst week.
The alumni want an hour of your week. Every week. For good.
Yes. They were here before me and will be here after.
Half of it, and I will spend the other half recruiting.
No. They get four evenings a year and my full attention at them.
Yes, and I bring two players every time.
You are fairly sure they have your signs. Two innings sure.
What do you do about it?
Change them, say nothing, and give them one wrong one first.
Change them between innings and never mention it.
I walk down there and say so, in front of everybody.
Nothing. If they have them they earned them.
Three catchers because one is hurt. It costs a bat every night.
Until he is healthy. You never want to need a third catcher.
Not another week. Somebody learns to catch by Friday.
It ends tonight. I would rather risk it than lose the bat.
It lasts. The two healthy ones are worth more rested.
Season over. Twenty-three men, a very quiet room, one thing to say.
Something about the four seniors, by name.
Exactly what we are going to do differently, starting Monday.
Nothing worth remembering. This is not the day for a speech.
That it was mine, and that next year will not be.
A senior can come back and start. The freshman you signed would not.
Yes. He earned a fifth year and the freshman has four.
No. I signed the freshman a promise and it was not a bench.
Yes, and I tell the freshman exactly what the year looks like.
Yes. Winning now is not a thing I apologise for.
You have just lost in a way you will think about at three in the morning.
Nobody. It goes in the car with me and stays there.
